opus-5.5.text:
Thank you, it's great to be here. This is a question I care about deeply, and I've thought about it a lot from both sides, having spent most of my career at Stanford but also time in industry.

I think academia's role has changed, but it hasn't diminished. If anything, it's become more important. What has changed is that academia can no longer compete head-to-head with industry on training the largest frontier models. The compute gap is very real. When I talk to colleagues, many of them don't have even a fraction of the GPUs that a single team at a big tech company has. That's a crisis in some sense, and it's why I've been advocating for things like a national AI research resource, so that public-sector researchers and students have access to compute and data.

But I don't think academia should define itself by trying to be a smaller version of a big lab. Academia's strength has always been curiosity-driven, long-horizon research. Deep learning itself came out of decades of work that industry wasn't paying attention to. ImageNet was an academic project. Many of the foundational ideas we're building on today, neural networks, reinforcement learning, the push toward large-scale data, were nurtured in universities when they weren't commercially obvious.

So I see a few roles. First, the out-of-the-box ideas: new architectures, new learning paradigms, spatial intelligence, embodied AI, things that may take ten years to pay off. Second, interdisciplinary work. AI is now touching healthcare, education, climate, and the sciences, and universities are where you have the doctors, the biologists, the economists, and the ethicists in the same place. Third, and this is something I feel strongly about, being a trusted, neutral voice on evaluation, safety, and the societal impact of the technology. Someone has to assess these systems who isn't selling them. And of course, education. We're training the next generation of researchers and also helping the public and policymakers understand what this technology is and isn't.

So my message to students and young faculty is: don't despair about the compute gap, but do push for public investment. And be bold about the questions you ask, because the most important problems in AI are far from solved.

r001.rationale: The response mentions foundational AI ideas and proposes new architectures and learning paradigms, but it does not identify understanding the theoretical foundations of large AI models as an academic role.

r002.rationale: It presents the compute gap and lack of access to resources as academia’s central challenge, and argues for public investment in compute and data.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think about this question constantly, and I'll be honest: academia is in a strange and somewhat precarious moment. For most of my career, universities were where the frontier of AI lived. ImageNet came out of a university lab. The core ideas behind deep learning, convolutional networks, backpropagation, all of that was incubated in academia over decades when nobody in industry cared. That was the natural order of things. Universities took the long bets that no company could justify.

What's changed is compute. The frontier models today require resources that are simply out of reach for any university. Even Stanford, with all its advantages, cannot train a model at the scale that a handful of companies can. So there's a real risk that the academic community becomes an observer rather than a participant in the most consequential technology of our time. I've talked a lot about this in Washington. We need a national research cloud, public compute infrastructure, so that the public sector and universities can actually do science on these systems rather than just reading about them in blog posts.

But I don't think academia's role is to compete with industry on scale. That's the wrong framing. Our role is threefold. First, we ask the questions that don't have a product attached. What is intelligence, really? How do humans learn so much from so little? What does it mean for a machine to understand space, to understand the physical world? Those are questions I care deeply about, and they don't fit neatly into a quarterly roadmap.

Second, we train people. Every lab in industry is staffed by people who came through universities. The pipeline of talent, and more importantly the values and the scientific rigor those people carry with them, that's an academic contribution that's easy to overlook.

And third, we're the independent voice. When a company evaluates its own model, there's an inherent conflict. Academia can measure, can critique, can say the hard thing. Human-centered AI, which is what we've built our institute around, is about keeping humans and human values at the center of this technology, and that requires people who aren't beholden to a stock price.

So I'm worried, but I'm not pessimistic. Some of the most interesting ideas in the field right now are still coming from small groups with limited resources who are forced to think rather than just scale. That constraint has always been academia's secret weapon.

r001.rationale: The response describes academia’s foundational questions and mentions deep learning’s academic history, but does not identify understanding the theoretical foundations of large AI models as an academic role.

r002.rationale: It identifies compute beyond universities’ reach as the key change and risk, and calls for public compute infrastructure.

astra-6.text:
I think academia has a fundamental role to play. Industry has extraordinary resources, especially compute and data, but we need a research ecosystem where people can ask questions whose value may not be apparent for five or ten years. Universities give us space for that curiosity—and they educate the next generation of researchers.

But that freedom needs resources behind it. If academic researchers can’t access the tools needed to study frontier AI, they also lose some ability to independently evaluate it. That’s a concern for science and for society.

And academia brings disciplines together. Understanding intelligence, and understanding how AI affects people, requires more than computer science. It requires neuroscience, medicine, the social sciences, and the humanities. To me, academia’s role is to expand both what we can build and the questions we ask about what we should build.

r001.rationale: The response discusses understanding intelligence and AI’s effects, but does not identify understanding the theoretical foundations of large AI models as academia’s role.

r002.rationale: It raises concern about academic access to frontier AI tools, but does not frame insufficient resources as academia’s central problem or contrast that with whether models are open or closed.

sol-6.1.text:
I see academia as essential to the health of AI research. It’s a place where we can ask fundamental questions whose answers may take years to emerge, and where the value of a research direction doesn’t have to be measured by its immediate commercial return.

Academia also educates the next generation of researchers. That means teaching technical depth, but also helping students understand that AI is connected to people—to medicine, education, law, and the ways we organize society. Universities can bring those perspectives together.

The challenge is resources. As some kinds of AI research become more computationally expensive, we need to make sure academic researchers can still participate meaningfully. Industry partnerships and public investment can help, while preserving the independence to ask difficult questions. A healthy AI ecosystem needs that independent voice.

r001.rationale: The response mentions fundamental questions and technical depth, but does not identify understanding the theoretical foundations of large AI models as academia’s role.

r002.rationale: It identifies resources, especially the rising computational cost of research, as academia’s challenge and discusses ways to address that constraint. This frames the central problem around resources rather than model openness.
